## Moving water through the plant is vital
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: right; width: 50%;">

* **Most transport materials dissolve in H~2~0**

<br/>

* **Water is component of photosynthesis**

<br/>

* **Water keeps cells turgid**
    + manipulated in guard cells

<br/>

* **Water is weird and cool**
    + heavy
    + viscous (thick & *sticky*)

 </div>

## Water has the capacity to do work: Water Potential
<hr>

* **Water has free energy (chemical potential) = ability to do work or move**
    + in botany = water potential ($\psi$)
    + $\psi$ of pure water = 0 (no solutes)
    + $\psi$ is generally negative but closer to 0 (higher) = more available energy

<br/>

* **$\psi$ determined by pressure, solutes & stickiness**
    + adding things to water (solutes) lowers water potential = -$\psi$
    + turgor in cells puts pressure on water (push) = higher $\psi$
    + tension on water in xylem (pull) = lower $\psi$

<br/>

* **Movement of water is related to water potential**
    + water moves towards more negative $\psi$ (more solutes)
    + cells interconnected = plant one big pond
    + $\psi$ gradient drives water into roots, transport through xylem, and movement between cells

<!-- <IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:250px; LEFT:750px; WIDTH:300px; HEIGHT:300px" SRC="images/beaker.jpg"> -->

## Plant cell walls will never burst!
<hr>

* **Example: Plant cells (-0.3 mPa $\psi$) placed in pure water**
    + water will move in to cell

<br/>

* **In plant cells, pressure builds up as the central vacuole fills with water**
    + The rigid cell wall resists expansion, creating turgor pressure (positive $\psi$).

<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 39%;">

* **This pressure raises the overall water potential (Ψ), often offsetting negative Ψs from solutes**
    + without the balancing pressure, water flow into cells until the burst

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:340px; LEFT:450px; WIDTH:600px; HEIGHT:350px" SRC="images/cellpressure.png">

</div>

## Phloem: uses active transport & water potential
<hr>
<br/>

* **Source: sites where sugars are exported**
    + active leaves or storage tissues

<br/>

* **Sinks: sites that receive phloem sap**
    + all parts of plant

<br/>

* **Sugars actively loaded/unloaded into sieve elements**
    + at source and sink (often using ATP)
    + changes water potential (Ψ at both ends)
    + water diffuses in/out driving sap flow
    + phloem under high pressure

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:650px; WIDTH:350px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/phloem.jpg">

## Xylem Transport: Soil - Root - Stem - Leaf - **Air**
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: right; width: 50%;">
**Water potential gradients are the driving force of how water moves through a plant**

<br/>

**Transpiration = loss of water through evaporation at the leaf surface**

<br/>

**The atmosphere to which the leaf is exposed drives transpiration because air has a really negative Ψ**

<br/>

**Creates a powerful negative pressure (tension) at the leaf surface, pulling water up**
</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:175px; LEFT:20px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/spac.png">

## Plant H~2~O transport: Soil - Root - Stem - Leaf - **Air**
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 47%;">

**Air controls transpiration by changing the water potential difference between the leaf and atmosphere, essentially sucking water vapor out of the plant when stomata are open**

<br/>

**Uptake: water moves towards more negative $\psi$**
</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:525px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/stemwater.jpg">

## Opening of stomata with sunlight creates the Ψ gradient
<hr>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:15px; WIDTH:525px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/stomata2.png">

## Cohesion-tension: Capillary action aids upward movement
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 42%;">

**Cohesion= water molecules sticking together via hydrogen bonding**

<br/>

**Adhesion=water molecules sticking to the walls of xylem vessels**

<br/>

**Combined create *capillary action (flow of liquid within narrow spaces)***

<br/>

**Allows water to rise through the narrow tubes of the xylem, against the push of gravity, as an unbroken column**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:530px; WIDTH:550px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/cohesion2.png">

## Capillary action + transpiration move water through plant
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

**Evaporation of water at leaves creates the transpiration pull (gradient of negative $\psi$)** 

<br/>

**This tension is transmitted down the whole water column due to cohesion**

<br/>

**This stickiness of water keeps the column of water from pulling apart**

<br/>

**When stomata are closed at night, cohesion/adhesion hold water in place**

</div>


<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:575px; WIDTH:450px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/cohesion-.png">


## Water pulled through root cells towards the xylem
<hr>

**Pull of water under tension in vascular tissues means xylem have a more negative $\psi$ than root cells**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:250px; LEFT:50px; WIDTH:1000px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/apoplast_symplast.png">

## Ψ gradient in roots cells drives osmosis
<hr>

**Due to the $\psi$ gradient in cells, the surrounding soil has a higher $\psi$, driving diffusion into root hairs**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:250px; LEFT:50px; WIDTH:1000px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/rootwater.jpg">


## Are there limits to moving water through plants?
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:600px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/vessels.jpg">

<div style="float: left; width: 52%;">

* **Really large trees (redwoods) can move hundreds of gallons of water a day**

<br/>

* **Gravity**
    + gets harder to move water vertically
    + xylem less efficient @ top
    + theoretically, limits growth to 122-130 m

<br/>

* **Drying soil adds more tension**
    + $\psi$ gets more negative, reducing the water potential gradient with the plant

</div>

## How can trees grow over 100 meters tall?
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 40%;">

* **H~2~O also pulled in zig zag motion**
    + pits in vessels/tracheids
    + tracheids are twisted

<br/>

* **Vascular tissue is tough**
    + high resistance of lignified walls
    + built not to collapse
  
<br/>

* **Coastal redwood tree nears theoretical limit!** 
  
</div> 

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:475px; WIDTH:600px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/vessels_pits.jpg">

## Issue: When the column of water breaks, embolisms form
<hr>

**Cavitation is the formation of air bubbles inside xylem vessels or tracheids, blocking water transport**
<br/>
**Occurs when tension (from transpiration pull) becomes too great, overpowering cohesion**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:240px; LEFT:5px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/embolism.jpg">

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:240px; LEFT:525px; WIDTH:550px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/embolism2.jpg">

## Fix: Can plants repair embolisms?
<hr>
**A stem would need to create a new $\psi$ with surrounding cells (via adding solutes) to refill while also compressing the air bubble until it dissolves into solution. If/how they do it is a huge matter of debate**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:270px; LEFT:100px; WIDTH:900px; HEIGHT:300px" SRC="images/bubble.jpg">

## Avoidance: Taper xylem (make skinny) as tree gets taller
<hr>
**Decreasing xylem diameter as plant gets taller reduces cohesion tension and promotes adhesion**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:220px; LEFT:100px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/xylem_art_1.jpg">

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:600px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/pittermann.png">

## Issues: Leaves (stomata) are sensitive to VPD
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 40%;">

* **Vapor Pressure Deficit: difference between moisture in air and how much moisture air can hold**
    + if *high* then the air is 'drier'
    + combo of temperature and humidity
    
<br/>

* **High VPD creates massive pulling effect for transpiration**

<br/>

* **If stressful, stomata *should* close**
    + stop excessive water loss

</div> 

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:500px; WIDTH:550px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/gs_vpd.jpg">

## Issue: What happens if if doesnt rain for a while?
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

* **If the soil dries out, what will &psi;_soil_ become?**

<br/>

* **Generally, predawn &psi; is really high**
    + right before sun comes up
    + stomata closed

<br/>

* **During day: stomata open, air pulls and soil water drained**
    + &psi;_soil_ become?
  
<br/>

* **How is this sustainable?**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:225px; LEFT:600px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/predawn.png">

## Fix: Soils will refill without rain
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 55%;">

* **Capillary action and surface attraction draw in water**
    + clay soils have lots of 'pore' space
    + often stronger than gravity

<br/>

* **Potential energy (aka water potential) governs how water moves around in soil**
    + redistribution @ night
    + 'sponge' behavior during day

<br/>

* **Prolonged drought can impact the soil water potentials**

</div> 

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:650px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/soil2.png">
